work.title: Roog
work.first_sale: November 1951, to Anthony Boucher for The Magazine of Fantasy & Science Fiction — Dick's first professional sale

source.note: Locator into the git-ignored reading corpus. No primary text is stored here.

reading.synopsis: Boris, a large black dog belonging to the Cardossi family, barks a single word — 'Roog' — at figures nobody else can see. The reader is given the dog's understanding from the first line and never leaves it. The Roogs are thin, white, unsteady creatures who come to the fence, study the yard, consult a map, and speak of the garbage can as an 'offering urn' and of Boris as a 'Guardian'. They are conducting a survey: this area is 'none too good for a first trial', too many Guardians, and a decision has been taken elsewhere by an unnamed 'They'. On Friday morning the Roogs arrive with their truck, take the offering, and — the story's central gesture — look up at the bedroom window where the Cardossis are sleeping. Boris drives them back by sheer fury. They leave, remarking that the truck is full enough this week and that they will be glad when this particular Guardian is finished. Meanwhile the Cardossis discuss giving the dog away, because the barking annoys the neighbours.

structure.form: continuous short story in five scenes across three days, hinged on the arrival of Friday
movements: Before dawn: a single Roog scouts the yard and sniffs at the window; Boris drives it off.
Daylight domestic interlude: Alf Cardossi tells the dog to put his tongue in and reads nothing in his distress.
Noon: two Roogs on the fence discuss the offering urn, the Guardian, and their map. The world's scale opens.
Evening: the Cardossis decide the barking is a nuisance and consider giving Boris away.
Friday morning: the collection. The Roogs look up at the window. Boris drives them back and is left howling.
structure.point_of_view: third person but aligned with the dog's construal throughout. The narration never adjudicates between Boris's reading of events and the human one. This is the whole technique of the story.

characters.name: Boris
characters.role: the dog; a 'Guardian' in the Roogs' vocabulary
characters.note: The only character who understands what is happening and the only one who cannot say so. His single word does all his speaking.

characters.name: Alf Cardossi
characters.note: Kindly and wholly deaf to the emergency. 'I sure wish I knew what is on your mind' is the story's most quietly devastating line.

characters.name: Mrs. Cardossi
characters.note: Tracks the dog's distress accurately — she notes it peaks on Friday mornings when the garbage men come — and draws the wrong conclusion from a correct observation.

characters.name: The Roogs
characters.note: Bureaucratic rather than monstrous. They carry a map, follow a decision made by others, work to a schedule, and are mildly irritated by an obstruction.

settings.name: The Cardossi yard and fence
settings.note: The entire theatre of the story. The fence is the boundary Boris polices and the Roogs cross at will.

settings.name: The bedroom window
settings.note: Where the threat actually points. That the Roogs look up at it is the story's only real event.

settings.name: The garbage can
settings.note: 'The offering urn' — one object under two irreconcilable descriptions, which is the story's engine.

motifs: The single word that means everything to its speaker and nothing to its hearers
The offering urn: the same object as refuse and as tribute, never reconciled
'Guardian' as a role the dog holds without anyone in his household knowing it exists
Friday as a recurring appointment — the horror is scheduled and routine
Smell as the sense that carries truth where speech fails
reading.significance: The device Dick would use for thirty years is already complete at 1,794 words: two mutually exclusive accounts of the same events, both internally coherent, with the narration declining to arbitrate. What makes it work is that the reader is never given a way to check. Nothing in the story confirms the Roogs are real and nothing confirms they are not; the dog's terror and the Cardossis' irritation are equally well evidenced. The garbage men are either garbage men or they are surveyors of a food supply, and the text will not say.
reading.closing_note: The Roogs' final exchange — that they will be glad when this Guardian is finished, and that they should leave something for next week — converts the story from an incident into a process already underway. Boris wins nothing; he defers.

concepts.note: A thin concept signature, which is itself informative: the story's charge is structural rather than lexical. It does not reach for the Exegesis vocabulary because it does not need to.

thematic_links_proposed.basis: two incompatible construals of one set of events, left unadjudicated
the one participant who perceives correctly is the one denied standing to report it
the story is precisely poised between perception and delusion and refuses to resolve

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Dick returned to this story across thirty years, and his account of it changed from a craftsman's note into something close to a personal reading of his own life.

evidence.source: Selected Letters — to Anthony Boucher and J. Francis McComas, 8 November 1951
evidence.quote: people who read it are disturbed, and go off brooding, very puzzled and unhappy
evidence.reading: Dick's own defence of the story, at twenty-two, on its acceptance. He is describing an effect, not a meaning — and the effect he names is exactly the unresolvable quality the story is built on.

evidence.quote: "Roog," as you slyly guessed, is my first acceptance.
evidence.reading: Establishes the biographical fact: first professional sale, to Boucher, in November 1951.

evidence.quote: I think the dog, who cried, "Roog, Roog," was trying to warn me and Tony. I got the warning…
evidence.reading: Decades later Dick reads his own first story as a warning that was addressed to him and that he received. The fiction has become testimony about his life. This is a Lane B statement about a Lane A text and the two must not be collapsed.

evidence.quote: going from "Roog" to Scanner is intrinsically complete
evidence.reading: Dick treats the body of work as an arc with this story at one end. His own periodisation of his career, offered as a reason he need not add a final explanation to it.

pkd_on_this_work.caution: The Exegesis passage is Dick interpreting his own juvenilia through the frame of 2-3-74. It is evidence of how he later understood the story, not evidence of what he meant in 1951 — and the 1951 letter, which says only that readers are left puzzled and unhappy, is the better witness to that.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: The story was "Roog" (originally titled "Friday Morning"), and Boucher f…
evidence.reading: Sutin supplies the original title, which names the story by its schedule rather than by the dog's word — a materially different emphasis, and worth recording as a textual fact.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: the men who haul away the trash are really alien Roogs who thrive on the food packed in metal "offering urns"
evidence.reading: Sutin's paraphrase resolves the ambiguity the story preserves — he states the Roogs 'really' are aliens. Recorded here as a reading, not as a fact about the text.

evidence.author: Anne R. Dick
evidence.work: The Search for Philip K. Dick
evidence.quote: Phil sold "Roog," his first story, to The Magazine of Fantasy & S…
evidence.reading: Corroborates the sale independently of Dick's own account.

contradictions.summary: Sutin's paraphrase settles what the story leaves open.

claim_a.text: the men who haul away the trash are really alien Roogs

claim_b.text: the narration never confirms or denies the dog's construal; nothing outside Boris's perception is corroborated

contradictions.note: Not an error on Sutin's part — a plot summary has to say something. But the difference between 'really are' and 'are, on the dog's account' is the entire story, so both are kept.

contradictions.summary: Dick at twenty-two describes an effect on readers; Dick after 2-3-74 describes a warning addressed to him personally.
contradictions.note: Both are his. The later reading is retrospective and shaped by the Exegesis project; neither cancels the other.

open_questions: Who is the 'Tony' the Exegesis passage says the dog was warning? Anthony Boucher, who bought the story and died in 1968, is the obvious candidate given the sentence's proximity to the sale — but this needs checking against the surrounding Exegesis context before it is asserted.

The original title was 'Friday Morning'. Is there correspondence recording who changed it, and when? The 8 November 1951 letter says 'the new title is all right', which implies the change came from the magazine.
Dick calls the arc from 'Roog' to A Scanner Darkly 'intrinsically complete'. Does he say elsewhere what he took the two ends to have in common?
